title: Desert Amplification in a Warming Climate
problem: Previous evidence for desert amplification was based on a short, 34-year dataset, raising the critical question of whether this phenomenon is a true long-term signal of global warming or merely an artifact of short-term climate variability.
method: This study analyzes observed and projected surface temperature anomalies by grouping land into large-scale ecoregions based on vegetation index to quantify the inverse relationship between warming rates and ecosystem dryness and to identify the responsible atmospheric drivers like longwave radiation and water vapor.
task: The task is to analyze observed and projected temperature anomalies by ecoregion from 1950-2099 to investigate the causes and persistence of "desert amplification," where the world's driest regions exhibit the strongest warming.
innovation: This paper demonstrates that desert amplification—stronger warming over the driest ecoregions—is a consistent, long-term pattern of climate change, primarily driven by enhanced downward longwave radiation from a warmer, moister atmosphere as greenhouse gases increase.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Here I analyze the observed and projected surface temperature anomalies over land between 50°S-50°N for the period 1950–2099 by large-scale ecoregion and find strongest warming consistently and persistently seen over driest ecoregions such as the Sahara desert and the Arabian Peninsula during various 30-year periods, pointing to desert amplification in a warming climate.

Here I analyze the observed and projected surface temperature anomalies over land between 50°S-50°N for the period 1950–2099 by large-scale ecoregion and find strongest warming consistently and persistently seen over driest ecoregions such as the Sahara desert and the Arabian Peninsula during various 30-year periods, pointing to desert amplification in a warming climate.
Observed surface temperature datasets. This study uses the ensemble mean of three global gridded monthly surface air temperature (T2m) datasets: CRU38, GISS2 and NCDC39, for the period 1950–2013.

Satellite measured vegetation greenness data. This study uses enhanced vegetation index (EVI), an optimized vegetation greenness index measured by the MODerate resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite sensor8 for the period 2000-2013, to examine the spatial dependence of observed and projected surface warming rates on large-scale ecoregions.

CMIP5 simulations. This study uses historical and projected simulations of 26 global coupled atmosphere-ocean general circulation models (AOGCMs) developed for the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5)40. For the historical simulations, there are two groups: one with time-evolving changes in anthropogenic (greenhouse gases and sulfate aerosols) and/or natural (solar and volcanic) forcing agents (referred to as ALL) and the other with only natural forcings (referred to as NAT).
